analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote to approve major federal agency rules before they can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee: introduced with zero cosponsors in October 2001, it sat without action until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, an agency's most important rules—those Congress designates 'significant'—would not take effect until both the House and Senate passed a joint resolution approving the rule word-for-word. If Congress never voted, the rule would simply never happen. Congress could also use petitions backed by 120 House members or 30 senators to revise or revoke existing rules. Monetary policy by the Federal Reserve was exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries facing costly federal regulation would gain a powerful new tool: any major rule could be killed not by a vote against it, but by Congress doing nothing at all. Members of Congress would also gain a direct veto over agency rulemaking, shifting power from expert agencies back to Capitol Hill and, practically, to whichever committees and leaders control the calendar.

how_it_helps.text: A 'significant rule' could not take effect until Congress enacted a joint resolution made up solely of the rule's text, giving members a final say over major agency actions.
Agencies would have to submit the rule, its purpose, its cost-benefit analysis, and its legal interpretation to both chambers before it could become final.

If Congress failed to approve a rule, no court or agency could infer that Congress intended anything by its silence—a provision proponents said would prevent agencies from claiming congressional blessing.
A petition signed by 120 House members or 30 senators could force expedited, amendment-free votes to revise or revoke an existing rule.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules—clean air and water standards, workplace safety, consumer and financial protections—would bear the cost. Because a rule would die by default unless Congress affirmatively passed it, any stretch of gridlock would freeze new protections, and industries opposing a rule would need only to stall congressional action to defeat it.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal protections from regulation

drawbacks.text: The default is death: a significant rule would fail unless both chambers passed a resolution within tight deadlines, so congressional inaction—not a vote—would kill public protections, which critics of this approach have long argued turns gridlock into deregulation.

The bill bars all amendments and motions to recommit on the approval resolutions, meaning Congress could only accept or reject rules as written, with expedited procedures that bypass the normal committee process.

The 'no inference' provision would tell courts they cannot read congressional intent from Congress's failure to approve a rule, which could weaken judicial deference to agencies and complicate enforcement of existing law.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the mechanism concentrates power in congressional leaders and committees—the majority leader must introduce the resolution and the Speaker or majority leader sets the reporting deadline—so a hostile committee could bury a rule without any vote at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is democratic accountability: major rules that bind the public would need an affirmative vote from elected representatives. But the design makes inaction fatal, so the practical effect would be that any Congress unwilling or unable to act—especially a divided one—would freeze significant new protections indefinitely, while regulated industries gained a cheap way to stall rules they opposed. The accountability gain is real; the cost to the public's regulatory protections would likely be larger.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Judiciary and Rules Committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2003 without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Nick Smith of Michigan introduced the bill on October 31, 2001.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in part, to the Rules Committee on the day of introduction.
On November 27, 2001, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, and no further action was recorded.
The bill died there when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without a committee vote or floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal agencies kept their existing authority to issue significant rules after notice-and-comment review and congressional review under existing law, without needing affirmative approval from both chambers—so people who depend on regulatory protections are no worse off, and regulated industries did not gain the veto point the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and people relying on regulations

for.name: Rep. Nick Smith
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor: introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary and Rules Committees.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI) in the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referring the bill to its Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law; the bill never received a markup or a committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no cosponsors from either party—only a single Republican sponsor—so no partisan line ever formed on this bill.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (environmental, workplace, financial, and consumer-regulated firms)
industries.note: The bill would have let these industries defeat costly new rules simply by encouraging congressional inaction, since a rule would die unless both chambers affirmatively approved it. The public cost would be delayed or cancelled protections on air, water, workplaces, and markets.

Agencies would lose their ability to make significant rules effective on their own authority, subjecting every major rule to affirmative congressional approval. This is the accountability trade-off proponents intended.
